etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English rage, from Anglo-Norman rage, from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs (“anger, fury”). Doublet of rabies.

Displaced native Middle English wode, from Old English wōd ("madness, fury, rage"; compare Modern dialectal English wood (“mad, insane, furious, raging”)); and Middle English hotherte (“anger”), from Old English hātheort (“fury, anger, wrath, rage”).

quote.citation: 1697, [William] Congreve, The Mourning Bride, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act III, page 39:
quote.text: Heav'n has no Rage, like Love to Hatred turn'd, / Nor Hell a Fury, like a Woman ſcorn'd.

quote.citation: 1879, R[ichard] J[efferies], chapter 1, in The Amateur Poacher, London: Smith, Elder, & Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: They burned the old gun that used to stand in the dark corner up in the garret, close to the stuffed fox that always grinned so fiercely. Perhaps the reason why he seemed in such a ghastly rage was that he did not come by his death fairly. Otherwise his pelt would not have been so perfect. And why else was he put away up there out of sight?—and so magnificent a brush as he had too.

quote.citation: 1841, Ralph Waldo Emerson, “Self-Reliance”, in Essays: First Series:
quote.text: But the rage of travelling is a symptom of a deeper unsoundness affecting the whole intellectual action.

quote.citation: 1864, Samuel Greatheed, Daniel Parken, Theophilus Williams, The Eclectic Review (volume 7? volume 120? page 130)
quote.text: This rage for boulevardizing has destroyed the quaint, queer, pestilential streets of old Paris, through which it was our pleasure to wander many years since.

definitions.definition: (slang, US, Australia, New Zealand) An exciting and boisterous party.

quote.citation: 2013, Larry M. Edwards, Dare I Call It Murder?: A Memoir of Violent Loss, San Diego, C.A.: Wigeon Publishing, →ISBN, page 95:
quote.text: That evening, Felix and Trish Homer invited me to the Sundancer for "a bit of a rage."

quote.citation: 1609, William Shakespeare, “Sonnet XVII”, in Shake-speares Sonnets. […], London: By G[eorge] Eld for T[homas] T[horpe] and are to be sold by William Aspley, →OCLC:
quote.text: And your true rights be termed a poet's rage

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “(please specify the page, or |century=I to X)”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:
1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne, chapter 6, in The Scarlet Letter, a Romance, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, →OCLC:
quote.text: convulsed with a rage of grief

quote.citation: 1856 December, [Thomas Babington] Macaulay, “Samuel Johnson”, in T[homas] F[lower] E[llis], editor, The Miscellaneous Writings and Speeches of Lord Macaulay, new edition, London: Longman, Green, Reader, & Dyer, published 1871, →OCLC:
quote.text: He appeased the rage of hunger with some scraps of broken meat.

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English ragen, from Old French rager, ragier, from the noun (see above).

Displaced native Middle English weden (“to rage with anger”), from Old English wēdan (“to rage”), among other synonyms.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To act or speak in heightened anger.

quote.citation: 2019 April 25, Hannah Beech, “Sri Lankan Accused of Leading Attacks Preached Slaughter. Many Dismissed Him.”, in The New York Times‎[1], New York, N.Y.: The New York Times Company, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2023-01-24:
quote.text: When a Muslim politician held a 50th birthday party, he [Zaharan Hashim] raged about how Western infidel traditions were poisoning his hometown, Kattankudy.

definitions.definition: (sometimes figurative) To move with great violence, as a storm etc.

quote.citation: 1674, John Milton, “Book VI”, in Paradise Lost. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  S[amuel] Simmons […], →OCLC, page 152:
quote.text: Horrible diſcord, and the madding Wheeles / Of brazen Chariots rag'd; dire was the noiſe / Of conflict; over head the diſmal hiſs / Of fiery Darts in flaming volies flew, / And flying vaulted either Hoſt with fire.

quote.citation: 1892, James Yoxall, chapter 5, in The Lonely Pyramid:
quote.text: The desert storm was riding in its strength; the travellers lay beneath the mastery of the fell simoom. […] Roaring, leaping, pouncing, the tempest raged about the wanderers, drowning and blotting out their forms with sandy spume.

quote.citation: 1922 October 26, Virginia Woolf, chapter 1, in Jacob’s Room, Richmond, London:  […]  Leonard & Virginia Woolf at the Hogarth Press, →OCLC; republished London: The Hogarth Press, 1960, →OCLC, page 11:
quote.text: The two women murmured over the spirit-lamp, plotting the eternal conspiracy of hush and clean bottles while the wind raged and gave a sudden wrench at the cheap fastenings.

quote.citation: 2012 November 1, David M. Halbfinger, “New Jersey Continues to Cope With Hurricane Sandy”, in The New York Times‎[2], New York, N.Y.: The New York Times Company, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2023-04-04:
quote.text: Though the storm raged up the East Coast, it has become increasingly apparent that New Jersey took the brunt of it.

quote.citation: 2014 June 24, Samuel Gibbs, “Google Glass go on sale in the UK for £1,000”, in The Guardian‎[3], London: Guardian News & Media, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2022-10-24:
quote.text: Debate has raged over whether Glass and smartglasses like it have any viable real-world use cases for consumers, or are more interesting to businesses where workers need hands-free access to information.

quote.citation: 2016 January 25, Marina Koren, “The East Coast Digs Out”, in The Atlantic‎[4], Washington, D.C.: The Atlantic Monthly Group, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2021-07-24:
quote.text: As the storm raged, more than 85 million people—or more than one in every four Americans—were covered by some kind of blizzard or winter-storm advisory on Friday, according to weather.com.

definitions.definition: (slang, US, Australia, New Zealand) To party hard; to have a good time.

quote.citation: 2012 August 2, Simon Reynolds, quoting Nathan Messer, “How rave music conquered America”, in The Guardian‎[5], London: Guardian News & Media, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2023-02-13:
quote.text: These events are all about raging hard, getting as fucked up as you can. Not necessarily even about dancing, just being a face in this giant extravaganza.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act 2, scene 1], page 28, column 2:
quote.text: The King is come, deale mildly with his youth, / For young hot Colts, being rag'd, do rage the more.
